item.title: A new route to calculating gluon production in proton–nucleus collisions
item.description: In the theoretical study of proton-nucleus collisions, the colliding projectiles can be described as streams of color charges moving along their respective trajectories. These color charges couple to gluons, which then produce the particles that are observed in the final state (gluons and quarks, which eventually produce hadrons).

item.title: A carefully timed pair of light pulses can amplify the motion of atomic layers in a quantum material
item.description: The principle "Work smarter, not harder!" apparently also applies to controlling quantum materials with light. Many of their fascinating properties depend on how the atoms are arranged in the crystal. Ultrashort laser pulses can be used to alter these structures in a targeted way—the light first excites electrons, whose changed energy and dynamics exert forces on the atomic nuclei and can thereby set the atoms in motion. Such processes unfold within femtoseconds, a millionth of a billionth of a

item.title: A new superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit
item.description: A recent study published in Nature Electronics and carried out by researchers from nanoGUNE's Quantum Hardware research group, Quantum Motion, London Center for Nanotechnology, Imperial College London and the University of Cambridge introduces a new superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit fabricated in a commercial complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) process.

item.title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
item.description: By injecting “thoughts” directly into large language models, researchers are trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection. The post New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Testing Einstein's laws from the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea
item.description: Are the laws of physics truly the same everywhere in the universe? This fundamental principle, known as Lorentz invariance, lies at the heart of Einstein's theory of relativity. Yet some theories that seek to reconcile gravity with quantum physics suggest that it might not always hold. To investigate this possibility, researchers from the international KM3NeT collaboration analyzed 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events detected by KM3NeT/ORCA, a neutrino telescope located deep in the Medit

item.title: Physicists step closer to the 'Zeptoverse' after 42-year particle search
item.description: Physicists have found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it is expected to occur only around once in every 10 billion "beauty" particles. The result, from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), follows a search spanning more than 40 years and brings physicists closer to exploring the "Zeptoverse"—an unexplored world that exists at distances of a billionth of a trillionth of a meter, or a "zeptometer," where new particles and forces of nature may be hiding.

item.title: Exactly solvable model reveals how trapped light can create magnetic order in one-dimensional spin chains
item.description: A research team wanted to better understand how the forces between particles inside a material change. They discovered that by confining one-dimensional classical spin chains inside a mirror box cavity with light, they could force these magnetic particles to organize and undergo a phase transition. Their work provides the simplest exactly solvable examples showing that light can create new phase transitions with materials.

item.title: ‘Reverse physics’ could help bridge the classical and quantum worlds
item.description: Physics is generally built on observations, then the maths that supports them comes later. Columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan takes a look at an effort to reverse this and rebuild the laws of physics from the maths up

item.title: A single measurement makes quantum bits more reliable
item.description: Researchers at the University of Regensburg and their international partners have found a way to significantly reduce errors in quantum bits. In an experiment, they demonstrated that a single additional measurement before a series of quantum operations can cut the error rate by more than half. The results have been published in Applied Physics Reviews.

item.title: How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole?
item.description: Astrophysicist Shep Doeleman explains how capturing the first image of a black hole required a telescope the size of the world, and why the next goal is to create a movie. The post How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Scientists achieve record-breaking low temperature on China's space station, paving the way for new physics experiments
item.description: Matter starts to behave differently at extremely low temperatures, creating conditions ideal for studying quantum physics and new states of matter. Now, researchers from China have achieved a new low-temperature record aboard their Tiangong space station. Their research, recently published in Science, might lead to a new generation of experiments in quantum physics and precision measurements in space.

item.title: A Strange Quantum Theorem Has Killed Einstein’s Reality
item.description: Albert Einstein fought to save our everyday notion of reality from the strangeness of quantum mechanics. But those who set out to aid him keep poking holes in his argument. The post A Strange Quantum Theorem Has Killed Einstein’s Reality first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Electrical control of an unconventional quantum transport state demonstrated in a magnet for the first time
item.description: Researchers at Tohoku University and the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA) have successfully controlled a unique quantum phenomenon—the quantum-geometric nonlinear Hall (QgNLH) state—using electric current for the first time. The breakthrough was achieved by revealing and exploiting the coupling between the spin structure and the QgNLH state in an electrically switchable chiral antiferromagnet.

item.title: How palm orientation shapes spin characteristics in volleyball jump serves
item.description: A new biomechanical study has uncovered how elite volleyball players control ball spin during jump serves, offering fresh scientific insight into one of the sport's most decisive offensive skills.

item.title: After 40 years of searching, physicists find evidence for an ultrarare particle decay
item.description: Physicists at CERN report that they've detected evidence of a rare meson particle decay (B⁰→ µ⁺µ⁻) that occurs when the meson's beauty quark annihilates with a down-type quark. The pair decays into a muon and antimuon, which are particles similar to electrons. Because evidence for this decay helps test theoretical predictions from the Standard Model, physicists have been waiting for it since 1984, when it was first theorized.

item.title: When Einstein's gravitational waves meet Newton's tides
item.description: Newton's theory of gravity has described the tides accurately for centuries. But could a tiny trace of Einstein's general relativity also be hidden in them? In a new study, a mathematician at Freie Universität Berlin has outlined how a targeted approach could be used to search for effects of this nature.

item.title: Five things to know about guiding sound for better communication
item.description: Every time someone picks up a call, the phone does a quiet bit of translation. Incoming radio signals are converted into tiny sound waves that ripple across chips before being turned back into data.

item.title: Single molecules could provide the building blocks for future quantum networks
item.description: Quantum computers rely on qubits as their units of information. To connect them into a larger network across long distances, they need to transmit quantum information using light.

item.title: Finding the fingerprints of noisy distributions in random quantum systems
item.description: Imagine shuffling a deck of cards where some of the cards are fading just because of the way they interact with the external environment as you shuffle them. Your job is to figure out the interplay between the shuffling, or "imposed randomness," due to the way you shuffle your cards and how that relates to the fading as cards are exposed to the external environment.

item.title: Light-matter hybrids form supersolid quantum state at room temperature
item.description: Researchers from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) have observed a new quantum state of matter known as a supersolid in an exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate. Remarkably, the phenomenon occurs not at temperatures close to absolute zero, but at room temperature. The results have been published in Science Advances.

item.title: Fingernail-sized chip untangles mixed light into clean beams
item.description: Stanford engineers and colleagues designed a chip that can take a muddled mixture of light from multiple lasers and output clean beams of light. It's the first time researchers have demonstrated a device that can take in mixed, or partially coherent, light and sort its photons into a clear set of separate beams.

item.title: 一个诺奖大国，为什么还要劝年轻人读博士？
item.description: 2024年3月，日本文部科学省发布了一项博士人才行动计划，副标题相当直白：“博士をとろう”，意思是“去读个博士吧”。

item.title: Anthropic秘密推行“巴拿马计划”，AI对人类存在究竟能知道多少？
item.description: 人工智能正在获得前所未有的能力，去阅读人类留下的痕迹。它可以调取浩瀚典籍，连接分散档案，在数百万、数千万乃至更多文本之间寻找关系。随着这种能力不断增强，一个诱人的幻觉也随之产生：仿佛只要档案足够庞大，机器最终就能够认识人类本身。

item.title: 我与“基地”的十年：为何只做那些没人愿意做的药？
item.description: 在全球合作日益复杂、越来越多国家和机构优先考虑自身利益与短期问题的时候，我反而比过去更确定：全球健康领域那些被忽视的疾病，仍需要有人更加聚焦、更加长期地投入。

item.title: 在最前沿的人工智能学院，为什么还要“古法教学”？
item.description: 2026年10月25日，中国人民大学高瓴人工智能学院教授魏哲巍受邀在《知识分子》《赛先生》举办的“AI对数学家到底意味着什么”论坛发表演讲，并参与“科学四十人”圆桌讨论。本文是论坛系列的第四篇，前三篇分别为芝加哥大学教授邓煜、北京大学教授袁新意和北京大学教授孙鑫的分享。

item.title: 北大教授孙鑫：AI冲击数学，我的个人体验、反思与倡议
item.description: 2026年10月25日，北京大学北京国际数学研究中心教授孙鑫受邀在《知识分子》与《赛先生》联合举办的“AI对数学家到底意味着什么”论坛发表主旨演讲。本文是论坛系列的第三篇。

item.title: 数学家袁新意：面对AI，数学是科学的第一道防线
item.description: 10月25日，在《知识分子》《赛先生》主办的“AI对数学家到底意味着什么”论坛上，多位学者分享了各自对数学未来的观察与思考。他们谈论新的可能，也审视随之而来的风险；有人忧虑数学根基的动摇，也有人期待建立新的大厦。我们希望留下这些或悲观、或乐观的声音，让未来回望的人们仍能听见这个复杂而动荡的时期中，研究者的思考与争鸣。

item.title: 逝者 | 激光冷却先驱克洛德·科恩-塔诺季逝世
item.description: 2026年10月22日，法国物理学家科恩-塔诺季在巴黎去世，享年93岁。

item.title: AI尚未引发失业潮，但年轻人承受了第一波冲击
item.description: 2022年底ChatGPT问世以来，关于“人工智能大范围取代白领岗位”的焦虑迅速蔓延。

item.title: A New Map of ‘Empty’ Space Challenges a Tranquil Picture of the Galaxy
item.description: For decades, astronomers treated the interstellar medium as a static backdrop to the goings-on of the universe. Now, a wave of 3D mapping is bringing the interstellar medium’s dynamic nature into focus. The post A New Map of ‘Empty’ Space Challenges a Tranquil Picture of the Galaxy first appeared on Quanta Magazine
